name: Neck corset

lead: A neck corset is a stiff collar-style garment, usually leather or boned fabric, that encircles the neck. In fashion and subculture it gives an elongated neck line and an upright head carriage; in medicine similar braces support weak neck muscles.

The appearance payoff is direct while it is worn: the rigid band holds the chin level and visually lengthens the neck. Published research covers the medical version, such as a Japanese study combining a corset with lidocaine injections in dropped head syndrome, not the fashion version.

paras: Wearers pick a fitted collar and wear it as part of an outfit, often with high-necked or corseted clothing; short sessions are the norm in fashion and costume use. Medical corsets are prescribed and fitted by clinicians.

A tight collar may press on neck blood vessels and cause dizziness, and poor fit can irritate skin or nerves. Long-term immobilisation may weaken neck muscles. Specific studies of fashion neck corsets are limited, so these risks are inferred from medical cervical collars.

angle.text: While worn, a neck corset props the head level and lengthens the visible neck, a look associated with high fashion, goth and costume styling. The effect lasts only as long as the garment is worn.

lead: A neck corset is a rigid garment or brace that encircles the neck. In fashion and subcultural styling it creates a stylised, elongated neck and enforces an upright head position, while in medicine related braces support weakened neck muscles [1].

For appearance, the effect is mechanical and immediate: a stiff band under the jaw keeps the chin level and the neck looks longer. Designers including Thierry Mugler in the 1980s used leather neck corsets in fashion collections, and high collars and chokers have long been used to lengthen the neck line [1].

Published research on the device is medical. A Japanese study reported that combining a neck corset with lidocaine injections into the scalene muscles improved dropped head syndrome in people with Parkinson's disease and related disorders [2].
infobox: Leather, boned fabric; thermoplastic or foam in medical versions

paras: In fashion, neck corsets are leather or boned collars that function as statement accessories and appear in high-fashion looks, goth and steampunk outfits and cosplay [1]. In medicine, soft collars use foam and rigid braces use thermoplastics to limit movement [1].

Nineteenth-century precursors include the Thomas collar, developed by Welsh orthopaedic surgeon Hugh Owen Thomas to immobilise the neck, and Victorian high collars stiffened with boning or steel that lengthened the neck line [1]. According to Grokipedia, a neck-corset style emerged in leather and fetish subcultures in the mid-20th century and entered fashion in the 1980s and 1990s through designers such as Mugler and Westwood [1].

Tight neck corsets may compress carotid arteries or jugular veins and cause dizziness; other possible problems include skin irritation, allergic reactions to materials, nerve impingement and muscle weakening from long immobilisation. These are largely inferred from medical collars, as specific studies of fashion neck corsets are limited [1].

No studies of fashion neck corsets have been found. In a medical setting, a study in Clinical Parkinsonism & Related Disorders evaluated lidocaine injections into the scalene muscles combined with neck corset wearing for dropped head syndrome in people with Parkinson's disease and related disorders [2]. Grokipedia summarises it as reducing average neck flexion from 27.7 to 11.7 degrees [1].
